name: Neck-to-jaw angle (cervicomental angle) theory

lead: The cervicomental angle is the angle where the underside of the chin meets the neck, seen in profile. Forum frameworks say an angle of roughly 105 to 120 degrees gives a sharper, more attractive profile line, and use it as a target for improving the chin-to-neck look.

The angle depends on chin projection, submental fat, platysma tone, skin laxity and the position of the hyoid and jaw. Aesthetic surgery literature describes neck aging as including a widening of the angle, with fat, muscle, skin and bone approaches to treat it; none of the studies located gives a numerical ideal.

paras: People use it as a measuring framework: photograph the profile, measure the angle, and decide which factor to work on. Approaches discussed include fat loss, fillers or fat removal under the chin, platysma work and chin surgery, each covered in its own article.
As a measurement framework it carries no direct risk. Procedures that change the angle, such as injectables, fat removal or genioplasty, carry their own surgical and medical risks.

angle.text: Forum frameworks hold that a chin-to-neck angle of roughly 105 to 120 degrees gives a cleaner, more attractive profile line, and treat it as a target to work toward. Surgical literature describes the angle and how it widens with aging, but gives no ideal range.

lead: The cervicomental angle is the angle between the underside of the chin or jaw and the front of the neck, seen in profile. In aesthetic surgery literature, aging of the neck is described as including a widening of this angle along with submental fat accumulation, loss of mandibular contour and prominent platysmal bands.[1] In looksmaxxing frameworks, a "neck-to-jaw angle theory" holds that a sharper angle in a specific range, often quoted as roughly 105 to 120 degrees, reads as more attractive.

The angle is a topic in the plastic surgery literature on neck rejuvenation, which discusses combined approaches such as fat reduction, platysma work, injectables and devices.[1][2] Studies located for this article describe treatments and anatomy; none establishes an ideal numerical range for attractiveness.

paras: Wikipedia notes that a double-chin appearance can arise from excess fat or from a bony deficiency in which an underdeveloped jaw leaves the chin blending into the neck; fat-related cases may be treated by fat removal, and bone-related ones by genioplasty or jaw surgery.[3] A review of neck rejuvenation lists widening of the cervicomental angle among the changes of aging, together with submental fat and platysmal bands, and describes combining several procedures.[1]

Studies have examined treatments that affect neck contour, but none tested the community's stated angle range. A 2016 review and case series described combination neck rejuvenation.[1] A 2015 paper described a microbotox technique for the lower face and neck.[2] A 1990 retrospective study compared osteoplastic and alloplastic genioplasty and reported high patient satisfaction in both groups.[4] Craniofacial photographic analysis has also been studied for sleep apnea prediction, a different aim.[5]

The theory is used alongside discussion of chin projection, hyoid position and submental fat as part of profile assessment. No forum sources were available to document specific threads or claims here.
